08 Trigger Words Transcript

   pathwaytohappiness.com/courses/self-mastery-course-1/08-trigger-words/08-trigger-words-transcript

                                                                        May 11, 2019

Today’s topic is “Banned words”. Those are the words we’re going to learn to do without.
I think today’s topic really addresses two of Don Miguel’s four agreements: the first is
about being impeccable, the second is about doing your best. There are two big
traps we get into with those agreements. As wonderful allies, and guidance those
agreements are, often people also use them to beat themselves up with:

1) Take for instance the agreement “always do your best”. So often I’ve seen people use
that as a rationalization for setting the bar really high, as if what we always need to
strive for is some kind of greatness. And in that regard, the Judge in our mind sets up
the standard, which we’re supposed to comply with, but it doesn’t really have the
understanding of reality, of the day to day changes that we’re in, and of the other
priorities in our life. It expects that top level performance, and so it uses that concept of
“always do you best” to put the bar out of reach a lot of times, and really often has no
leniency and understanding for anything, but for that superlative performance. And
then we feel tired one day or we didn’t do that extra mile that our imagination set up as
a standard, and now we’re beating ourselves up because we didn’t do our best. So, we
haven’t really used the “do you best” agreement in the way that it’s intended, because
what it’s really intended to do is to neutralize that Judge in our mind that rejects our
self, and to give it the defending agreement, and say: “Hey, that was my best today,”
“That, giving my circumstances and my other priorities, and my day, and my week, is
what I was able to do,” – not to be used as an excuse, but to be used for a lot of self-
understanding and compassion, and not just for yourself, but for other people. To
realize that they are doing their best that they can with their myriad of priorities, and
not to let our expectations set the standard, that then the judgments follow on from. I
think some of that will be clear in today’s session.

2) The other aspect about the impeccability is that beating ourselves up and saying we
didn’t do our best, is a self-criticism. You might think: “Oh, no, I’m really trying to do
these four agreements, I need to try harder, I didn’t do well enough right there,” and
that self-criticism isn’t impeccable. Because that core meaning of “impeccable” is about
expressing our self without fault and without blame. That means no criticism, no
putting anything down. I’d be even seeing people to start that agreement and say: “Hey,
you’re not being impeccable,” and doing it in a judgmental way, as if others doing
something wrong, which is to say: “I’m finding fault with you, you’re not living by the
four agreements.” And then that impeccability becomes the standard that you’re
supposed to do your best by, and when you don’t, it’s a wide open door to self-criticism
from that inner voice of the Judge. Well, that self-criticism isn’t impeccable either.





                                                                                                                                1/11

The assignment I want to give you today about the banned words, has a lot to do with
dissolving this voice of criticism. It’s about undoing a lot of those critical judgments.
Now, we’re not going to do it all in one fell swoop, because over the years the Judge has
become a very strong archetype character in our mind, and from my experience it
doesn’t usually go away in a first week and a half. It’s got a pretty embedded place in
our mind. This is why there are a number of assignments that I give, that slowly chip
away at the foundation and the structure, by which it’s established itself. And this one,
you find, takes a lot of the structure away. It could take you quite a bit of the time, so be
patient with yourself and use this exercise as something to practice in the way of
mindfulness for the coming weeks, and months, and years. So good luck.

A little while back we had a discussion about “Finding neutral”, which is about
refraining from agreeing with people and disagreeing with people. Also I
mentioned to refrain from agreeing and disagreeing with your own opinions in your
own mind, which in Miguel’s book “The Voice of Knowledge” we would call “not
believing yourself” – one of his creative mulls to his apprentices, which means:
“Don’t commit to your own opinions,” “Don’t reinforce the structure of your belief
systems.” That’s the very belief system of the Book of Law, that’s a tyrant running our
life, and something that we want to dissolve. And if it’s something we want to dissolve,
we want to stop committing to it. Well, now we’re going a step further in that. We’re
going to eliminate certain words from our lexicon. And we’re going to do this because
these words are very powerful and are generally used against ourselves. And we’re going
to eliminate them until certain point, when we can use them much more impeccably.
But for now, using them, we stab ourselves more, and go against ourselves more than
we move in that direction of truth and love. So we’re going to put them on the “may
not use” list, until we get qualified to operate with them.

To give you an idea of the power of a word let’s start with something small. Let’s start
with the word “sail boat”. And just by giving you that word, in your mind you may find
likely a picture of the sail boat, you may know its color, whether the sails are up, if it’s
out at the see, if it has spinnakers running. And if I say “rose”, you may know whether
it’s cut or on a bush, what color is it, is it budding, is it blossomed, is it a rose someone
gave to us. Our picture is that clear. Each of those words, there’s a whole picture, and
that picture has a certain emotional content. A rose may bring you a certain wonderful
emotion. A sail boat? Maybe you had a bad experience out there in the water, and your
body cringes. Notice that there’s a whole picture, and you’re in that world in your
imagination, and there’s the rose or there’s the sail boat in front of you. So you create a
whole virtual reality with the whole world made by that one word. And often, there’s a
lot of emotion behind that certain word. If we use the word “money”. Money may bring
out the fear of scarcity, may bring out all sorts of reactions. Let’s use the words
“republican”, “democrat”, “liberal” or “conservative”. How much emotional charge is
behind any one of those words? The word “liberal”, for instance, or “conservative”.
There’s the word, but there are also all the agreements we have about the word, the
structure and the attitudes we have about the whole group of people. There’s all the
emotion that happens, and there’re all the experiences, all our points of view, our

                                                                                                                                2/11

opinions. If we use “liberal” or “conservative” about the environmental policy, economic
policy, foreign policy, social policy. Those are substructures of that one word “liberal” or
“conservative”, and it comes a lot with the whole lot of a battle of attitude, emotion and
mega stories. Now, that’s one word. Generally that one word brings us into a kind of a
conflicted state, mentally, emotionally. That’s the power of a word. It creates a whole
dream, and it gives a whole impression in one’s mind. And generally the emotional
response to those things is not pleasant, because we have so many agreements
structured around that one word. These are agreements we’re not even aware of, but if
someone asks us what we think, we’ll be all too ready firing opinions left and right on
these issues. Not that they’re really making us happy, but we have them.

Then I’ve created a list of banned words. Why are they banned? Because they’re
generally don’t serve us. They are actually the words that I’ve found that Judge uses
most often. That super critical, hanging Judge in our mind always condemns either
ourselves or someone else, or lifts someone else up above us, or lift ourselves up above
someone else. That Judge always works in those two directions of self-importance:
putting ourselves down below other people, making us the worst in the world, or lifting
ourselves up and saying we’re better than other people, we’re the best in the world, and
putting other people down indirectly. The banned words, as I call them. “Banned”. And
I don’t want to call them “bad” words, you’ll know why in a minute. These banned words
are words we are going to refrain from using. And I’ll give you another way to speak
instead. These banned words are such words as “good” and “bad”, “right” and
“wrong”, “good” and “evil”, ”suppose to” and “not suppose to” (that’s a term, not
just one word), “should” and “shouldn’t”, “better” and “worse”, “best” and
“worst”. These are banned words, these are words that we use to divide and separate,
and when we use it, it’s generally used from the point of view of the Judge. These are the
words that are the critical elements that Judge uses to put ourselves or someone else
down. These are the words that the archetype character of our Judge uses to create a
world of duality.

In Don Miguel’s book “The Voice of Knowledge”, he talks about Adam and Eve, and
they take the apple. What the apple represents is the knowledge of good and evil.
That knowledge of good and evil is the ability to describe some people as good and some
people as evil, meaning we can put a value placement on one group of people being
better than another group of people. We can also use words “good” and “bad”. We then
have the ability, through description, to divide people, making one group better and
another group worse. With those words we have the capacity to describe and divide
everything in the world into duality, into separate parts, raise one part up and put
another part down. As soon as we raise a part up, we put another part down, and we’re
saying: “This creation of God isn’t as good as that creation of God.” Once we’ve done
this, we then reject the lesser part. The lesser part is not good enough, it’s worse than,
it’s a reject material, it shouldn’t be around, it should be different. But we are only able
to do that because we abide by this structure of duality – words that I’m inviting you to
ban from your vocabulary. If we are to have peace in our own mind, we will have to
dissolve the Judge in our own mind, which means we will have to take away its

                                                                                                                                3/11

weapons. Its weapons are basically its words and its descriptions, and its
 stories that it uses against ourselves and other people. Once we’ve used these words
to divide the world up through description, then mind makes a further assessment and
says that those things that are “good”, “wonderful”, “right”, “should”, “better”, deserve
our love, and so we send our love in that direction. And those things that don’t meet that
half of the list, those things that are “worse”, “not as good”, “bad”, “evil”, those are the
things that we rationalize sending our emotional poison, hatred, anger, disdain,
rejection to. These might just be the aspects of ourselves where we decide: “Ok, we’re
not going to send our love to that aspect of our self, cause we hate that part of ourselves,
cause that part of ourselves is not good enough.” Maybe it’s our body. Cause we say it’s
overweight, and we say: “It’s not what it supposed to be,” “This isn’t the body I’m
supposed to have.” We reject it and we use that word, and the whole structure, and the
power of that word as a means to justify not sending our love and our gratitude in that
direction. In this way the structure of these words sets up in our mind the whole
paradigm of conditions, of how and when to love and when not to love. It sets up the
structure that allows us to be angry and hateful or upset, or frustrated, when our body
isn’t doing what it’s supposed to do, when someone at work did something they
shouldn’t have done, when our partner didn’t do something they were supposed to do.
These are the words we’re used to rationalize not being loving, not being kind, not being
respectful.

These words that I’m offering you, these banned words, go to the heart of the way the
Judge divides the outside word or divides our self form the world, makes us “worse
than”, “not good enough”, makes us “better than someone else” or “better than
everybody else”, and in doing so we divide ourselves and we feel alone, and we miss that
communion with humanity.

I’m asking you to make a list of banned words, and you can add some. Along with “bad”
you can put “terrible”, “disgusting”, whatever your words for “bad” are; “weird”,
“strange”. And there are other words like “good”, “to be moral”, “ethical”, “just” and
“fair”. Those are words we use to describe things that are good, and by doing so we also
put a dividing line and say: “OK, those other things are bad.” Consciously or
subconsciously they are there. Whether we recognize and consciously create a list of bad
things or not, subconsciously they are at least there. The division has been set up, and
what we’re saying is that one part of God’s creation is better than another, and this
worst part “is all wrong”, “is all messed up”, and that then becomes enough reasoning
and excuses not to love. And as long as we find things not to love, we are not happy,
because happiness is our love, our gratitude coming out of us. That’s how it’s created. So
if we take away all those divisions, and everything is the same in the way we love it, it
doesn’t mean we have to agree with everything, but at least we are not allowing the
Judge to come in and create a divider, to stop our love from coming out of us.

Now we need to make a clarification. If we don’t use these words, what are we going to
use? This is where our conversation goes from being opinion generated by the Judge to
sharing our point of view. Cause the point of view doesn’t really have the same

                                                                                                                                4/11

structure of agreements, it doesn’t have the duality, it doesn’t have the absolute right
and wrong, fair and unfair, good and bad, that those words imply. Take, for instance, we
go get ice cream, and I ask you what kind of ice cream you want, and you say:
“Chocolate-chip,” and I say: ”Why?”, and you say: “It’s the best ice cream!” Well, is that
exactly true? Is that the best ice cream? It’s not the best ice cream to me. I like Cookies
& Cream. So, Chocolate-chip is the best ice cream for you. That doesn’t make it the best
ice cream. In your point of view it’s the best ice cream. Why is it the best ice cream for
you? Because you like it the most. Then, we can say: “Why do you want Chocolate-
chip?” – we want it because we like it the most. That’s why we want it. Not because it’s
better than any other ice cream. Because if it was the best ice cream, then everybody
would like it. But not everybody does, it’s purely a matter of personal preference, hence,
“31 flavors”. That’s why they are so well established. Because not everybody has the
same favorite ice cream. Otherwise it would just be called “1 flavor”, but it’s not. It’s
called “31 flavors”. It’s “31 flavors”, because everybody has a personal preference, a
personal point of view of what is their favorite, of what they enjoy the most. And it
doesn’t make another flavor bad or less than any other flavor. And it’s not that you
should or shouldn’t have a certain flavor, because it’s not about having the right ice
cream or wrong ice cream. It’s about having the right ice cream for you. And the right
ice cream for you is the one that you enjoy. Instead of saying: “I want Chocolate-chip
because it’s the best ice cream,” we say: “I want Chocolate-chip because I enjoy it the
most.” So, Chocolate-chip is the choice not because it’s the best, not because it’s good,
but because I enjoy it the most. And that’s different. That’s a preference, that’s a
personal point of view. That’s not an absolute opinion. If we take a political side, and
someone says: “I agree with this political philosophy,” and you ask me: “Why?”, I will
tell you: “Because it makes the most sense to me, I like their approach.” That’s a
personal point of view, that’s a preference. But you noticed that I don’t use the words
“Because they’re right in the way they manage the monetary policy,” “They are correct,”
or “They are moral.” I’m not saying they have the right moral and social values. No, I’m
not using the word “right”, I’m using the term “I agree with,” “I feel most aligned with.”
Now it’s just a personal preference. I choose it because it’s the right choice for me. And
in the right choice for me, it doesn’t have to be the right choice for anybody else. I’m not
making that judgment. You notice that if I say: “It’s right,” – that’s a judgment
assessment and my Judge has absolutely huge opportunity to make someone else wrong
or reject some other policy or philosophy, and my Judge has such a foundation to
operate from. But if I let go of those words, and I move out of the absolute opinion of
“OK, this is absolutely right, and not only is it right for me, but it’s right for everybody,
because it’s the right thing to do,” to saying: “This approach makes the most sense to
me.” Now I’m saying things in a way where I am not trying to impose my agreements
structure of what is right or wrong on anybody else. If they have a different policy they
buy into, if they have a disagreeing structure, they are not going to feel like I’m in
conflict with them. I’m not trying to put out the whole structure of what is right or
wrong, good or bad, and impose it on the top of your structure. I’m only sharing: “In my
dream, in my world, this is the way I see it. And for you, you tell me how you see it, and
we don’t have to agree. We don’t have to decide who is right.” In this world of points of


                                                                                                                                5/11

view, everybody is allowed to have their own point of view. Once we try to state things in
terms that are absolute: “This is right” and “This is wrong,” meaning “It’s not just right
or wrong for me, but this “right and wrong” structure applies to everybody,” – now
we’re trying to put everybody in the same box, and we’re trying to give the same law that
we have in our Book of Law to everybody else. And for sure other people don’t want to
live by your Book of Law, so they push back, and they try to condemn your version of
right and wrong, good and bad. Now we have conflict, because our Judge has used the
word of right and wrong, good and evil, to divide our self by belief system from other
people. And now we have conflict with other people. Not because we’re in conflict, no,
us humans we’re the same, but because we have different beliefs and our beliefs are
in conflict. Then, if we don’t make our beliefs right and we don’t make them wrong, we
don’t make them good or bad, we don’t make other people good or bad, our
conversation becomes more neutral, and all we do is share our point of view. And we
don’t have to make anybody else’s beliefs right or wrong, or good or evil. In this way
everybody can have their own beliefs without conflict. In this direction we move our
whole conversation, and our attitude, our point of view to respect. Where we respect
everybody and their own point of view. The way we do this is to let go of all those
banned words, those kinds of words that I mention that divide things up in right and
wrong, good and bad, terrible and best, those types of words. And we start to use words
like: “I enjoy this one the most,” for what we like and what we don’t like, “ I agree
with this approach,” “This is what I like,” “This makes the most sense to me,”
“The way I see it is,” and that’s where it gets a little dangerous, because we can start to
then say: “The way I see it is…” and then give a whole opinion about what’s right or
wrong. But words that we can easily move to: “What I enjoy,” “What works for
me.” Not “What’s the best,” but What works for me,” not “What’s better,” but “What
makes the most sense to me.” We’ll find out if we apply these kinds of shifts in words, in
conversations, at work, at our relationships, we will find ourselves having a lot less
conflict, because we bring our point of view to something, instead of our opinions which
are absolute.

The conflict is really between beliefs. Two people have two opposing beliefs, and
each one is defending this conceptual ideas of “right” and “wrong”. They each think
their own ideas are right, their own policies are right, and then, if that’s the case, any
other policy, any other idea that doesn’t agree with that is thrown by them into the other
category of duality as “wrong”. So now we have two people with two points of view,
based on two completely different assumptions, and they are fighting with each other
because they are both defending conceptual ideas. But without that conflict in
conceptual ideas, they would have nothing to argue about. So, the cause of the conflict is
really the conflict in ideas. And this is a fundamental conflict around the world. This
conflict is in that people are defending conceptual ideas and fighting each other
personally over them, when they are just conceptual ideas. And we can have conflict
in our own mind that says: “I should go do this,” “Oh, no, I shouldn’t go do that,”
“Oh, yes I should go do this,” “Oh no I shouldn’t go do that,” and we can have two
conflicting beliefs in our mind. One that says we should go do something, and another
one that says we shouldn’t. And each argument has its own point of view, has its own set
                                                                                                                                6/11

of assumptions, and so, depending on what point of view we take and what set of
assumptions we want to apply, we get a different conclusion. Well, this is how we create
a conflict in our own mind. And if we can do it in our own mind, we can certainly do it
with other people, cause there it’s quite a bit easier to have two separate points of view.
So, if you’re having a conflict like that, it’s based in two different points of view, which
have two different sets of assumptions that create two different paradigms. And now
you have the conceptual ideas that don’t match up. They don’t agree with each other.
But you see what they are formed from, you see the basis of the conflicts that’s really in
different points of view that have different assumptions. That’s what creates the
conflict. And so many of these conflicts are based around these words that we’re
learning to ban here in this exercise.

Forming our statements using these banned words is like stating an absolute
criteria. If we ask: “What’s best?”, or if we say: “This one is better,” we’re saying
something that is absolute. By “absolute” I mean that by that description of better or
worse, or best or better, we’re saying: “This is how it is in the world.” This way, our
description of what we’re looking at is being expressed as if it’s absolute for everybody,
as if it’s the right thing to do, and not just for us, but for everybody. Once again, if we
say: “This is the right thing to do,” we are saying that this is the right thing for anybody
and everybody to be doing. It’s implied. It’s not said, it’s not meant, but when someone
else hears it, they assume that that’s the law, and that’s the law that’s being applied to
them, and if they have a differing opinion, they may assume: “They think I’m
wrong,” or “They think I’m some version opposite in that realm of duality of
what they are,” or “I’m not meeting their criteria, therefore I’m not good
enough,” “I’m not meeting what they feel is right, therefore I’m wrong.” So,
the way that minds interpret entire paradigms of value when we use those words in an
absolute way, has a huge impact both on ourselves and on other people emotionally.
That’s why much of what we do in this exercise, and what prevents dividing the world
and creating the duality, is about describing things in terms of point of view, instead of
terms of absolute, which is how these words are often used.

I had a client who was doing this exercise, and he was driving to a new town with his
wife, and while following the directions they missed the turn off. And they had the
conversation: “Oh, was that the right turn?”, “Should I have taken that exit?”, and he
realized he was using the word “should”, and he started asking himself: “Well, should I
be using the word “should”?”, “How else can I ask: “Should I make that right turn
there”?” Well, he was asking this according to the directions, but let’s look at how
subjective the terms “right” and “wrong”, not in terms of the “right” and “left” direction,
but in terms of “right” and “wrong” may be. Is it the right turn? Well, according to the
directions, it was the right turn and they missed it. But what if there’s constructing
works on the road, that the internet directions didn’t provide, and you end up being
backed up for an hour? Well, then it’s the wrong turn, based on the constructing works
on the road at that specific time. But what if you go a little further down the road, and
you take the next exit, circumvent the construction, and now it’s the right direction
because this way gives you a better time, but it’s the wrong exit according to the map?

                                                                                                                                7/11

What if you go one exit further, and now it takes a lot more time to get there, but that
exit takes you through a scenic route of beautiful trees, and it becomes a very

power in the way that we could use it as a judgment. Because then we can look at

they shouldn’t be doing that,” we can catch ourselves and realize: “Hey, my
assessment is based on a point of view,” “My assessment doesn’t take into
all account the factors that that other person is considering. So, let me step
aside and hold off from my judgment, and let’s understand their paradigm
first as to why they made those choices.” And now we are listening a lot more and
accusing a lot less, and we’re understanding that other people are doing their best,
according to their criteria and their decision making process, and we don’t have to put
the emotional charge on there that the terms “better” or “best”, or “worse” usually come
along with, and this can do a lot to change our emotional state.

What this all about is a lot of little shifts in language. And it looks pretty small. But
these are extraordinarily shifts in how we communicate and interact, these are life
changing shifts in our relationships, and in how we see the world, and in how we see
ourselves, because if we take away the words that the Judge uses the most to divide us,
whether from other people of from ourselves, then we no longer have the reasons not to
love and appreciate, and respect, then we open the door to experiencing, perceiving and
interacting with the world in a completely different way. Rumi shares a wonderful story
in his poetry, and it goes to the effect that if there is the field out beyond the right doing
and wrong doing, and he refers to this field as “endless, unconditional love”, and he
says: “I will meet you there,” but first you have to move past, go beyond the fields of
right doing and wrong doing, to let go of that voice of knowledge that divides
everything, until you see the whole world as one living being, no better and no worse
but itself.

If we go back to those strong words like “liberal”, “conservative”, “loyalty”, “betrayal”, or
whatever word you say, they can pull us into a whole dream that has a whole point of
view, and it divides everything up to who was right and who was wrong, what was fair
and what wasn’t fair, and it locks us in a certain point of view. Just that one word
“betrayal” can pull us back to the entire experience when we felt betrayed, or maybe we

                                                                                                                                8/11

feel like we betrayed somebody else, and we feel guilty and shame for having done
something. And that one word “betrayal” divides ourselves and other people into the
categories of who is right and who is wrong, who is fair, who is unfair, who is good and
who is evil, and it splits everybody, and we put ourselves on one side of it or another,
and we do it to our own emotional detriment. Those words go against our emotional
integrity. And that is what I call “the real betrayal”. We betray our own emotional
integrity by taking that point of view and saying: “They wronged me, I was right,” or “I

When I talk of things this way, I’m giving you a whole new paradigm for how we may

view that we’ve built up for ourselves in the past. There’ll be a time again when we can

but for now it’s about dismantling the structure that the Judge has created and the
Victim has created, and letting go of those points of view that those words pull us into.
Just to say: “I shouldn’t have done that!” – we are putting ourselves down. What if
instead we said: “I now know I had a different way to do that that will be more

awareness of how I would do that differently,” – we are integrating that lesson
and improving ourselves with our awareness and evolution, and growth, but we’re not
convicting, condemning and punishing ourselves by the Judge, simply because we no
longer use that word “should”.” We can say: “Ok, I can see where this didn’t work very
well this time,” – that’s clearly saying: “This thing that I did, didn’t work.” It doesn’t

in their use that they are going to come out of our mouth, and they are going to come
out in our thinking. And this is where it’s time for us to catch ourselves when we use
those words and go: “Aha, there it is, now I see it, let me rephrase that.” Instead of
saying: “I shouldn’t have done,” we can now say: “OK, now with this awareness of
the results of that action, I can see there’s a more effective way to do this,
that I will endeavor to do next time.”

There are places where we will use the word “good” or “right” at times: if we’re having a
wonderful piece of chocolate cake, we can say: “This is so good.” Mmm, be more precise
to say: “I’m enjoying this,” or “This tastes really good,” and even more precise and
preferable: “This is really enjoyable.” Because you know, the chocolate cake that you

                                                                                                                                9/11

think is so good, someone else may not like. So we could say: “This is really enjoyable
and tasty to me,” – slightly different, but has a huge impact if we could speak this way
with awareness.

I had someone who was doing this assignment, and he wanted to know if he could use
“to make the “right” turn” or “”left” turn”. Yes, there are places we can use the term
“right”, that actually means the direction as opposed to the “left”. This is different from
the terms “right” and “wrong”.

There’ll be a time when we can use these words again, about what we should be doing
and shouldn’t be doing with our lives, about what we’re supposed to do and not
supposed to do. But for now these words are so corrupted, and they are so powerfully
used by our Book of Law, that pretty much whenever they are used, they are used
against ourselves. So, make it your endeavor, make it your new law to break with that
old Book of Law that’s been a tyrant, and refrain from using these words, and find a
different way to communicate, that is more precise, that has a more personal point of
view approach, and expresses your personal preferences, without projecting your book
of law out into the world or to other people. And you can apply this to your own
thinking. Even the thoughts in your mind when you catch yourself saying: “Oh, gosh, I
screwed that up, I wasn’t supposed to do that,” or “Oh, God, I got that wrong,” you
could say: “Aha, so i get it wrong,” or you can say: “I saw that I didn’t act
skillfully there, and the result wasn’t what I intended.” We’re making the same

perpetuating an unworthiness emotion and a whole point of view that comes with that
structure, every time we declare or agree with the idea that we were wrong, or that
somebody else was wrong. That’s the power of words. Instead of saying: “I was wrong,”

That’s going to have the completely different emotional quality. Your assessment is the
same, but that word “wrong” isn’t there, and so it doesn’t pack that emotional punch in
the gut. And that’s going to change your emotional state, and that’s going to change
your point of view, just by letting go and no longer using these banned words.

The second great benefit of this is that we’re taking these words out of the hands of the
Judge, who’s wielded them against ourselves and other people for so long. This is a big
step in dis-empowering the Judge archetype character in our mind. And we’ll do more
that dissolves the Judge as time goes, but doing this, this disarming, taking these
weapons of words out of the Judge’s hands is huge. I mean what’s the Judge going to do
when he can’t divide up and make us better or worse than anybody else? And it can’t
make the world better or worse. It can no longer split people as “better” or “worse”,
“good” and “bad”, “right” and “wrong”. If we refrain from that, that Judge character is

                                                                                                                           10/11

dissolving away. If we’re not buying its stories anymore, we’re no longer committing to
those stories, cause we’re no longer committing to those words, and we’re finding a
whole new channel of communication – one that is based on respect for other people’s
points of view, and the channel of communication that doesn’t use our words to go
against ourselves.

This exercise will also give you the added benefit of watching every word that comes
out of your mouth. That level of awareness to watch every thought that goes
through your head, and to catch it and say: “OK, let me restate that that way without
those words. I need the assessment part of that comment, but I don’t need the value
judgment, the rejection part.” Just hunting these words in your internal dialogue and
your external communication will heighten your awareness and that awareness alone
will help you to change your conversation and communication, change the way you use
your words, so that you become much more impeccable.

Pathway to Happiness

08 Trigger Words

We’re moving all courses to the new Self Mastery Community


Watch Video At: https://youtu.be/Lf0yUMrZQMs

Summary of practice

1. Listen to the Trigger Words lesson audio
You may want to listen multiple times.

2. Watch for the use of those words in your word and thoughts. Noticing is
half the process. A list of the words is below in the questions area.

3. When you notice the use of those words, try to rephrase what you are
thinking or speaking in a clearer way without the trigger words. Do your best
to ban them from use for a while.

4. Journal about how those trigger words were used by you in speech and
thinking. Write out the character that used that word or phrase. Write out what the
emotion or attitude that went with the thought that had the trigger word in it. You are
learning to hunt how your mind has structures of thoughts with emotion and attitudes
embedded in them. These structures are held together in your unconscious. You are
making yourself consciously aware of the unconscious. This is how deep change
happens.

Some notes

As you find banned words, it is likely that they have some emotion behind them. That’s
a good find. At this point I suggest making note of what Character (from the last
assignment) is using the banned word. This way you can continue practicing the
Character Hunting journal writing while you notice Banned Words.

This might help to hold your attention on the exercise by making it more interesting.
This all works to keep your attention in the point of view of the Observer or Hunter.


                                                                                                                                   1/4

Do you get the idea that maybe this is all going somewhere? Perhaps there is a overall
plan of attack for all these exercises. That maybe they somehow work together. I like to
think so.

You are observing and hunting for the banned words. They are going to trigger your
conscious mind that an unconscious pattern is happening. You find the phrase, and see
how a character is using it. Then look for a way you can say or think more clearly, and
change it. In the meantime you also become aware of the character behind your
language, and the emotion.

You are practicing all the skills of Attention, Shifting Identity to Observer, Skepticism to
recover personal power, and moving out of the emotions. More on the emotions and
what to do about them in the next exercise.

Banned words may not seem like a big deal. They are just a bunch of words. How are
using or not using some words going to change my life? Because those words form the
structure of your belief paradigm about yourself. Specifically they go to the conceptual
structure of agreements that the Judge and Victim character maintain. They also shape
the way we see the world according to this paradigm. For example, take a look at how
we might see our false selves.

Our “not good enough” stories use words like bad, worse, wrong, failure,
loser, shouldn’t, and not supposed to.

Our “good enough” image uses words such as good, better right, success,
winner, should, and supposed to.

These words form the basic materials for your imagination to create images in your
mind and aspects of your self worth and identity. If you eliminate the words you
eliminate the story lines. When you eliminate the story lines you disrupt the false
images and the minds neural pathways. You false images are structured in this belief
paradigm of duality. What you are doing is creating a perception and feeling of freedom
from your mind’s limiting paradigms.

Bringing the lessons together

In the meantime, keep journal writing going. Write about what the characters say, do,
and what the emotions are. If you don’t see them in real time, then write in the third or
even first person format. Then read what you wrote and see what different characters
are in there. Edit, or re-write it to include emotions and attribute characters to the
thoughts, having the emotions, or doing the behavior.

Write about which character uses the trigger words you notice during the day. Write
about what other characters might have emotions connected to those words, or build a
reaction thought to the trigger word.



                                                                                                                                   2/4

Resistance to change

A good way to dismiss an assignment, an opinion, or something you don’t like is to first
unconsciously exaggerate it out of proportion. Then, in the exaggerated form, you can
easily find something to dismiss as a problem, wrong, bad, or not reasonable.

You may find a character that thinks things like: “Does Gary mean we can never use
those words?” These are exaggerated statements. Some words that might be flags for
this are “never”, or “always”.



I’ve already given two exceptions to the banning of trigger words. It’s okay to give
yourself some other exceptions too.


For instance, maybe you don’t do the assignment on the weekends. Or you do this
assignment until you get through the last session of the basic series.

It’s okay to limit the use of this exercise in ways that work for you. Also know that after
you break your unconscious uses of language, that you can go back and reclaim the
words and meaning of those words in a more truthful and conscious manner later.

For me I now will commonly use the word “should”. However it is very different that
what it used to mean. It used to mean following the rules of the judge is what I “should
do”.

Now, stuff I should do is aligned with what makes me happy. For instance, I might say,
“We should go get ice cream.”

It’s a nice way to use those words, but I had to break the habit of the judge using
language against me first.

Common questions

Is there a way to use those words that would be okay?
Yes. There are many. It is largely a matter of meaning and the emotions those words
have packaged in them. Those trigger words, or banned words are used extensively by
the Judge and Victim. This exercise is about taking ammunition out of their hands.

You can even corrupt the phrase “I love you.” Just say it with sarcasm and you have
packaged toxic emotion and attitude in those three words. Banned/trigger words have
lots of unconscious toxic attitude and emotions.

This exercise will help you become aware of how you use language and what you are
really communicating.


                                                                                                                                   3/4

What are the words we are banning?
Should, Shouldn’t

Supposed to, and Not Supposed to

Good, Bad

Right, Wrong

Good, Evil

Better, Worse

Best, Worst

Are there other words that are trigger words to be included?
Yes, you can include other high duality words, or words that have an emotional charge.
Certainly ban cuss words, as they tend to express rejection.

However, for now, you might make the assignment more focused, and just focus on the
ones given. After you are good at leaving these out of your lexicon you can level up in the
game and subtract some more.

Supporting videos


Watch Video At: https://youtu.be/pKOPQE0bfaw

Trigger words and resistance

It’s a search for a door way where larger changes can happen. After you find these
trigger words and how they activate reactions, you can look for other words, or
behaviors that activate your emotions.

Watch Video At: https://youtu.be/vfEPGw4H_K8

Bringing together the elements of attention, the concept made of words,
imagery in the mind, and perspective.

Language is imprecise and symbolic. It fills our mind with misunderstandings.
